title: Tree seedlings in eastern US forests followed about 58% of their spatial temperature slope in 1999-2025, saplings and adults under 25%; the seedling shift did not follow local or regional warming
abstract: Question: community thermal composition follows only a small part of its spatial temperature gradient in time. Is demographic inertia (longevity) the cause? Trees test this: seedlings turn over in years, adults in a century. Data: USDA Forest Inventory and Analysis annual plots in 31 eastern US states, natural forest only (209,534 visits on 64,508 plots, 1999-2025), and NOAA nClimGrid temperature. Method: cross-fitted species temperature indices from adult occurrence; a presence community temperature index (CTI) for seedlings, saplings and adults; spatial slope b inside 2-degree blocks; within-plot CTI trend; tracking ratio R = trend / (b x warming trend), where 1 is full space-for-time response; local, regional and 70-year warming contrasts; exact species terms; 2-degree block bootstrap. Results: all layers had similar spatial slopes (b 0.63-0.65 C per C). Plots warmed 0.22 C per decade. Seedling CTI increased 0.083 C per decade (R 0.58, 95% CI 0.38-0.84; 0.47-0.74 in core-species, genus, weighted, stand-age and undisturbed variants). Saplings gave R 0.08 (-0.09 to 0.26) and adults 0.17 (0.07-0.28), or 0.24-0.25 after a stand-ageing adjustment. But the seedling shift did not follow warming differences: consecutive-visit local warming gave R 0.03 (-0.07 to 0.14), and across 101 blocks the regional R was -0.60 (-0.84 to -0.30). Only the 1951-1980 to 1996-2025 warming offset was positive (seedling minus adult CTI 0.26 C per C, 0.41 of b). The seedling increase came mostly from fewer seedlings of cool or locally cool species (red maple, sugar maple, black cherry, aspen, paper birch); dogwood loss and ash regeneration acted against it. Adults warmed because cool species died faster than they grew in (mortality -0.17 C, ingrowth -0.10 C relative to standing adults). Conclusion: the fastest layer moved near its spatial expectation, so longevity alone does not set the gap; the shift stops at the seedling-to-sapling step. But a trend near the spatial expectation is not proof of climate tracking, because it did not follow where warming was larger. Limitations: short span and small warming contrasts, US-only STI ranges, perturbed coordinates, FIA protocol changes, unmeasured browsing and pathogens, several tests added after a 12-state pilot (which gave seedling R near 0).

display.caption: (a) First-visit community temperature index (CTI) of seedlings, saplings and adults against plot 1981-2010 temperature (1 C bins, pooled slope b in legend). (b) Tracking ratio R by layer and test, 95% 2-degree block bootstrap intervals; dashed line is full space-for-time tracking. Seedlings follow about 0.5-0.7 of their slope in the trend tests but not in the local or regional warming tests. (c) STI of ingrowth, natural mortality and harvest relative to the standing adult CTI at the previous visit.
Year effects (plot and year fixed effects) of seedling, sapling and adult CTI, 1999-2025, with the full-tracking path b times the 10-year trailing temperature year effects (dashed).

Exact species terms of the within-plot presence CTI trend for seedlings (a) and adults (b), 8 largest positive and negative terms; species STI in brackets. A positive term for a species that is cooler than its plots means that the species became less frequent. See species_contrib CSV files for presence trends.
